claims.text: High configurational entropy causes local lattice distortions that enhance electron–phonon coupling and thereby cause superconductivity.
The superconducting state is a conventional isotropic s-wave state in the dirty limit.
Superconductivity remains robust and has a well-defined transition despite strong chemical disorder.
The selected alloy is initially in an as-cast state.
The starting material is an equiatomic or near-equiatomic multitransition-metal alloy with random site occupation on a simple lattice.
A temperature window below approximately 10 K is appropriate for detecting the anticipated superconducting transition.
Random atomic-size and bonding-environment variations produce subtle local lattice distortions.
High configurational entropy produces a random but homogeneous chemical disorder.
Entropy-induced lattice distortions enhance the electron–phonon coupling needed for Cooper-pair formation.
Anderson's theorem protects the s-wave superconducting state from the alloy's disorder in the dirty limit.
Reducing configurational entropy by substitution or chemical ordering will reduce the beneficial local lattice distortions.
Reducing the local distortions will weaken electron–phonon coupling and lower Tc.
The high-entropy starting alloy will have a higher Tc than the reduced-entropy variant.
The high-entropy starting alloy will have a sharper superconducting transition than the reduced-entropy variant.
A chemically similar reduced-entropy alloy should exhibit weaker or absent superconductivity.
The proposed mechanism is limited to alloys with conventional s-wave pairing and moderate electron localization.
Extremely strong disorder can localize carriers and invalidate the proposed superconducting mechanism.
Magnetic impurities or other pair-breaking effects can invalidate the proposed mechanism.
The quantitative influence of entropy-induced distortions on Tc and the balance between scattering and electron–phonon coupling are not established.
The superconducting response may vary with alloy composition and processing history.
